en: Salutation to the infinite Viṣṇu, the root of existence, consciousness, and bliss; the cause of the sprout of the universe; eternally risen and ever-full. || 1 ||

I shall proclaim the conduct of the virtuous, which is pure and auspicious, and woven together with the established conclusions of all the Vedāntas, for the sake of the yogis' attainment of knowledge.
At dawn, I remember the splendor of the divine Savitṛ, the Self;
that which is most excellent, may he inspire our thoughts toward bliss. 3.
Through positive and negative concomitance in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep,
that which is the one, absolute consciousness— that alone am I, the supreme, the vast.
This play of knowledge and ignorance ceases through knowledge within knowledge;
having abandoned both knowledge and ignorance, only pure knowledge remains. || 5 ||
The body is exceedingly impure, while the embodied self is exceedingly pure;
knowing "I am unattached," this they declare to be purity.
The mind, like a fish, sports eternally in the ocean of bliss;
by means of the water of perfect realization, it is well-bathed and its self is purified.
Then, one should perform the Aghamarṣaṇa rite by restraining the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
fixing the mind in complete concentration like a submerged jar in the ocean.
When the mind is free from worldly craving at the junction between stillness and distraction, that junction has been mastered by him; he is liberated, of this there is no doubt.
The recitation always occurs at all times within the body of every living being;
by realizing "I am He" (Haṃsa So'ham), one is liberated from all bonds.
Satisfying one's own senses with one's own happiness is true contentment;
by perceiving the mind with the mind, the Self shines forth by itself.
One should cast the mind as a single oblation into the self, which is the fire of self-luminosity;
he should be known as a true performer of the Agnihotra sacrifice, while others are merely bearers of the name.
The body is said to be the temple, and the embodied soul is the stainless deity;
when worshipped with total devotion, it shines forth through one's own direct experience.
Silence, self-study, meditation, the object of meditation, and the contemplation of Brahman—
through knowledge, there is the vision of reality due to the complete cessation of these two [pairs].
I do not remember nor do I contemplate anything of the past or the future;
free from attachment and aversion, I experience whatever auspicious or inauspicious occurs here.
Indeed, renunciation is the constant practice regarding the body, not merely the wearing of ochre robes;
the certainty that "I am not the body, I am the Self" is the defining characteristic of renunciation.
The wise say that the gift of fearlessness to all beings is the highest;
lack of desire for anything other than one's own bliss is considered the ultimate limit of dispassion.
One should engage in the hearing of the Vedānta and reflection through logical arguments;
then, through yoga, one should practice constant repetition, and from that, the vision of the Self arises.
Because the power of words is inconceivable, direct cognition arises from the word alone;
just as a sleeping person is awakened by the word itself. (19)
Through the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, knowledge becomes unwavering;
the disciple, enlightened by the Guru, transcends the Śabdabrahman.
You are neither the body, nor the senses, nor the vital breath, nor the mind, nor the intellect;
because they are subject to modification, are perishable, and are objects of perception, just like a jar.
Pure, absolute knowledge, without distinction and stainless—that which is the one supreme bliss, the non-dual reality, "That thou art. (22)
The beginning and end of sound are established as that very [Self], and the same is true for the mind;
in the middle, it always exists as the witness—abandon your delusion regarding that very Self. (23)

The identity of the gross and the Virāj, the identity of the subtle and the Hiraṇyagarbha, the identity of ignorance and Māyā, and the identity of the inner self and the fullness of consciousness. || 24 ||

In Viṣṇu, whose singular essence is pure consciousness and whose nature is the identity of Brahman and the Self, the world has arisen through mere delusion, just as the illusion of a snake arises in a rope. (25)
The wise, however, know that for the logicians (tārkikas), these two—the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa)—are both the primary denotations (vācya);
whereas according to Sāṅkhya and Yoga they are the implied meanings (lakṣya), and according to Vedānta there is their identity (aikyatā).
Having abandoned those two aspects denoted as cause and effect— the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa)—
it does not abandon their two signified (lakṣya) aspects, which are the portions of consciousness (cidaṃśa) and are of a single nature.
Where is knowledge in the treatises on ritual action? There is no certainty in logic at all.
Sāṅkhya and Yoga have fallen into division; the grammarians are intent only on words. (28)
All other heretics are extremely difficult to find in any news of true knowledge;
only the singular realization of Vedānta shines forth through one's own direct experience.
"This is I" and "this is mine"—this is bondage; "I am not" and "this is not mine"—this is liberation.
Bondage and liberation appear through the qualities (guṇas), for the qualities arise from primordial nature (prakṛti).
The one consciousness always shines, stainless in all states;
those of meager fortune do not know its own nature, which is purely vast.
He who knows that "I am indeed that knowledge which is the witness of volition and the sole life of all the worlds" is liberated; there is no doubt about this.

For one to whom the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and likewise the resulting cognition appear as manifestations, what need is there for a means of knowledge for the sake of knowing? (33)
The mental modification (vṛtti) takes on the form of the object; through its fruit, the object is revealed.
One cognizes the knowledge of the object, and that very object is revealed. (34)
Let it be that [the object] is merely pervaded by the mental mode (vṛtti); how could there be pervasion by the fruit (phala)?
For the conscious self (cidātman) is of the nature of self-luminosity and is already established. || 35 ||
The mind becomes conscious through its conjunction with mere consciousness;
it moves within to proceed from one object to another object. (36)
That state which is without support and free from modification is known as *sonmanī*;
one should understand that when the mind (*citta*) is devoid of the letter *ta*, it becomes consciousness (*cit*). (37)
The letter *ta* represents the superimposition of objects, like the redness of lac on a gem;
through the abandonment of the object of knowledge, knowledge remains in its absolute purity. (38)
The triple fold comes to an end and one attains the extinction of Brahman;
all this is mind alone, and that mind is nothing but knowledge. (39)
They say that ignorance is delusion and supreme knowledge is the highest state;
they call this ignorance, as well as false knowledge, "māyā."
One should know the Lord as the wielder of *māyā*, yet as transcending *māyā* and stainless;
in the sky of consciousness which is eternal bliss, the mind is like a fleeting cloud within the mist of *māyā*.
There, the ego-sense is the thundering and the mental fluctuations are indeed the torrential downpours;
in this darkness of great delusion, the Lord rains sportively.
To bring an end to that rain,
the wind of awakening is the knowledge of the nature of the seer and the seen, and the higher realization (vijñāna) is the emptiness of the seen.
Brahman alone is one and non-dual; there is no diversity whatsoever here.
Knowledge of the field and the knower of the field—that is knowledge; that is said to be true knowledge. (44)
And the unity of both—the individual knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self—is vijñāna;
while knowledge derived from the scriptures is parokṣa, and vijñāna is the direct vision of the Self. (45)

Knowledge (*jñāna*) is that which has the meaning of "thou" (*tvam-artha*) as its object—the Self (*ātman*), which is Brahman, properly divested of the two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); and higher knowledge (*vijñāna*) is that which rests upon the word "that" (*tat-pada*). (46)
The realization of the identity of the two feet is designated as knowledge (jñāna) and higher realization (vijñāna);
the wise call this the knowledge of the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self. (47)
In this world, ignorance is one thing and consciousness is another; yet the universe consists of that [consciousness].
Through positive and negative concomitance, one perceives it as the single reality everywhere. 48.

That knowledge which arises from mental modification is consciousness (*vijñāna*), while mere knowledge (*jñāna*) alone is the wisdom that destroys ignorance; thus, wisdom (*vijñāna*) possesses the nature of both. || 49 ||
This [soul] is established in knowledge and discernment, and its offering is in That, the True Brahman;
the enjoyer is the pure quality of sattva, while rajas is the means for enjoyments.
They say that the quality of darkness (tamas) is the object of enjoyment, while the Self (ātman) among these is the illuminator;
he is ever devoted to the study of the Veda and intent upon the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya).
He who knows that "all is Brahman" is called a *brahmacārī*;
the householder is one who abides in the midst of qualities; the body is said to be the house. (52)
"The qualities perform the actions; 'I am not the doer'—thus thinks the wise one.
Of what use are fierce austerities for him whose austerity consists of knowledge? (53)
He who is free from joy and resentment is called a forest-dweller;
he is a true householder who has transcended the home, for the body is said to be the home.
The wise person who constantly adheres to this code of right conduct is swiftly liberated from the ocean of worldly existence; of this there is no doubt. (55)

Thus ends the *Sadācārānusandhāna*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya*).
